From experience we all know that these permissive clauses very seldom amount to much and particularly with a body which has now so much to do and before which there will be more and more cases coming as time

goes on. It is not at all likely nor is It in human nature that the board would wish to take up these matters unless they are brought to its notice. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals claims that because this House has given the commission power to deal with these matters, therefore, this House should leave the commission alone. The commission is the creature of this parliament and if there is something in the Act which ought to be remedied, I cannot see that that is any argument why this parliament should not provide the remedy. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals deliberately neglected lo express any opinion on the merits of this question, and it seems to me that that is the fair way for the members of this House to consider the question which is of so much interest to the people at large. No doubt, towns and villages differ, as the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals stated, in their requirements, but at the same time I do not know of any town or village in which it is right or proper that a railway company should run a train at the rate of forty or fifty miles an hour without protection for the public ; and certainly the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals did not give us the name of any such town or village, even if he knew of one himself. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that something ought to be done to make it easier for the public to get their rights. I am sure that in so far as the actual wording of the Bill is concerned the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and others of more experience will be able to say whether it ought to be worded exactly as it is, but I certainly feel that it is right for this House and the government to take this matter into their consideration and pass some such legislation of a general character as will meet the requirements of the case. I do not think that the people ought to be left to come to the commission and fight out these matters in detail as they now have to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure we all agree with the object which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) who introduced this Bill had in view ; that is to say the fuller protection of life and property at level crossings throughout the cities, towns and villages of Canada. At the same time it is important for us to realize what the legislation at the present time is and to ascertain, if possible, how far an improvement in the direction which my hon. friend wishes to go and in which we sympathize with him, would be accomplished by the legislation that he has introduced. It seems to me that it is impossible to imagine that this House could possibly incorporate a railway company that would not at some point pass through a city, town or incorporated village, and in passing through a city, town or incorporated village of necessity it must
cross some one of the highways in these cities, towns and villages. What is the law in such a case ? The law is that no railway can cross a highway in any city, town or village except with the previous consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and the law is that this Board iOf Railway Commissioners must determine the conditions under which this railway can cross the highway. Now, if the railway is already in existence over the highway it is still within the power of the Railway Commissioners to alter the conditions under which that railway crosses the highway ; so you have in the' Board of Railway Commissioners at the present time the power to determine the conditions under which the crossing is to be made and the power to regulate a crossing already in existence.
But they do not do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend will exercise a little patience, please. What did my hon. friend seek to do by his legislation, and what would be the effect of the legislation he is introducing ? There should be, it seems to me, no doubt that railway crossings must of necessity exist under different conditions, and you must deal with each crossing in the light of the local conditions. For instance, you would not pretend to regulate a crossing in the heart of a great city in the same way and to make it subject to the same conditions as you would a crossing in the outskirts of some obscure village. You must bear in mind the conditions existing at each crossing. What would be the result of the proposed legislation if we adopted it 1 The result would be that the Railway Commissioners would not have a free hand, but that they would be obliged to determine that at each railway crossing, whatever might be the local conditions, there must be either one of two things-either a watchman or a gate. No discretion is to be exercised if the crossing is in the heart of Montreal, or, as I said, on the outskirts of some obscure village anywhere throughout the Dominion of Canada. The conditions of crossing would require to be settled by the Board of Railway Commissioners in absolutely the same way in all caShs.
How is it now ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Now it is subject to the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners.
But under a condition imposed by parliament ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not quite understand.
As to speed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the absence of regulations, the speed cannot exceed 10 miles an hour.
But they can regulate ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They can regulate that speed so as to make it less than 10, or they may permit them to proceed at a higher rate, provided that proper precautions are taken at the crossing.
Can the Board set aside a law of parliament ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, they can, when the law provides that they shall have the power to do so.
Does it provide that power ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, it does ; the section-No. 186, I think-says that positively.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that if I have stated the conditions correctly, namely, that the Board of Railway Commissioners have the power to determine the conditions under which a crossing can be made on the level, then the only question to be considered further by this House is as to whether or not the Board of Railway Commissioners can be moved to interfere in each particular case. It is not necessary that the Board of Railway Commissioners should deal with each case in each municipality, but it is free to the Board to determine the conditions under which all the level crossings in any municipality shall he regulated. They shall have the right to determine the conditions for the whole municipality at one time. And then the question comes up as to whether or not it Is an obligation on the individual to go to the Board of Railway Commissioners and complain of the conditions existing at each crossing, or whether or not by some other method the Board can be moved to take action. Let us see what happens.
Nothing happens.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As a rule, the conditions are that a railway crossing is dangerous to all persons in a particular locality. No one individual is affected by that exclusively, but dozens of those who use that crossing are affected, and as a result those individuals would all of necessity make application to their municipal council. Through this body the municipality would act; if a railway crossing dangerous to the life of the individual existed within the municipality, the corporation of the municipality would take action, and, if the corporation did not take action, we all know how prone our electors are to go to members of parliament, and if they draw the attention of members of parliament to the fact, all the members would have to do would be to draw the attention of the minister to the existence of the dangerous crossing, and then the Act provides that the minister, of his own motion, can set the machinery of the Board of Railway Commissioners in action and have the matter regulated, so that you will have either the individual con-

; cerned with the crossing acting through the [* municipal council, or else they can act - through their member, and in this way >
bring pressure to bear on the minister. It seems to me that these are conditions which , would commend themselves to this House,
' and that the members will see how reasonable it is to allow this matter to be dealt , with by that Board which this parliament * has created for the purpose of dealing with questions of this sort. I quite understand that it is exceedingly important that public attention should be drawn to the conditions existing at these crossings, and espe-; cially that the attention of the Board of : Railway Commissioners should be drawn, and this discussion is an important diseus-: sion from that standpoint. It is important that the Board should know, as they will learn as a result of this discussion, that these dangerous railway crossings exist at different places, and that parliament expects them to provide a remedy for these dangerous conditions. My suggestion would be, under the circumstances-because, after all, this is an important matter, and affects not only the individuals and municipalities, but the railway corporations as well-I know it is not popular in this House to speak in the interests of railway corporations, but, so far as I am concerned, at all events, I think that a railway corporation is entitled to justice as well as a municipality or an individual-I consider that under the conditions that arise here, it is proper that we should refer this matter to the Railway Committee, so that the Railway Committee may hear all those who are interested further, and if further light comes to us it is possible that we might all change our minds and endeavour to introduce legislation which would be effective if it is necessary to do so. I would therefore concur in the second reading of this Bill, with the understanding that it should go to the Railway Committee for further consideration.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
Hon. CHARLES FITZPATRICK (Minister of Justice) moved that the Bill be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. A. LANCASTER (Lincoln and Niagara).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before that motion is put, 1 desire to say a word or two. Those of us who were in the House last parliament will remember that many public bills were referred to the Railway Committee, and nothing came of any of them. No amendment was made unless a Bill was considered and dealt with in the Committee of the, Whole House, as Public Bills are supposed to be dealt with. I remember that the hon. member for St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers) introduced very necessary legislation imposing on railways responsibility for fires caused by locomotives along the line

or their railway, and making them liable for damages to the people whose property along the railway was injured by such fires. That Bill was introduced in two different sessions and sent to the Railway Committee, but nothing came of it on either occasion. When we were considering in the House the general Bill consolidating the general Act that amendment Became law. Then Mr. Cowan, who represented Essex, introduced in two different sessions a Bill relating to drainage under railways, legislation which was very much needed in the interests of the farming community, particularly Ontario. That Bill was sent to the Railway Committee each session, but nothing came of it until, in 1903, we were considering in the Committee of the Whole House the Bill to consolidate the General Railway Act, when it, too, was adopted and became law.
I could instance other Bills. For in-stance, the Minister of Agriculture, in introducing any measure relating to his department, does not suggest that it should go to the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization. If he wants the Bill passed, if he is sincere, as I presume he is, and as I am to-night, he insists, as I do, upon the Bill being dealt with as all Public Bills are, by being referred to the Committee of the Whole House. I could instance many other cases. When the Minister of Justice last session introduced an amendment to the Railway Act, the same Act that I am endeavouring to have amended to-night, he did not say that he wanted the Bill to go to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines, although the railways were interested in that Bill to a much larger extent than they are in mine, in order that the railways might be heard on the question, and that those who were against the railways might also be heard. He took the regular course of moving that the House go into Committee of the Whole on the Bill. It was dealt with as all Public Bills are; it was discussed in Committee of the Whole House and there only. What was right with regard to the Minister of Justice amendment to the Railway Act of 1903 is equally right with regard to the amendment of the member for Lincoln to the same Act. I submit, with all due deference, that this Bill ought to be dealt with by the Committee of the Whole House, and not be sent to the Railway Committee. That committee is only a cul (ie sac. a place that leads nowhere. The Bill must come back here. Suppose the committee endorses it, it has to come back here [DOT] and be dealt with by the whole House. Suppose, on the contrary, the committee say they do not think it ought to be passed, still it must come back here; they cannot keep it out of this House. It is only tying up the Bill for the session, as was done in the case of the cattle-guard legislation which was introduced by me for three sessions and was always sent to the Railway Committee and
smothered there-always killed in some way, but not on its merits; and finally the amendment was passed when the House was in Committee of the Whole on the General Railroad Consolidation Bill of 1903. With all these facts before us, with this knowledge, to which we cannot shut our eyes, as to what happens to public legislation that goes to the Railway Committee, I object to this Bill being sent there. I am not referring to Private Bills, which properly go there, and which, if condemned there, do not come back to the House at all. But Public Bills, properly so-called. I submit, should not be sent to the Railway Committee, and this Bill should be treated like all other Public Bills. There should be the same rule for all of us. We should now go into Committee of the Whole House and discuss this Bill; and I think we could put it into better shape than we could by wasting our time in the Railway Committee, having a lot of discussions and votes and hearing railway counsel and other people, who after all can tell us nothing that we cannot learn from our constituents. We are supposed to make the laws as we understand that our constituents want them ; and if the Minister of Justice or myself or any one else in this House wants to know what the views of the railway companies are, we are honest and intelligent enough to find them out as part of our duty, just as we find out the views of the rest of our constituents-because the railways are as much our constituents as other people. I submit, therefore, that we should deal with this Bill on the floor of this House, as we do with all other Public Bills. I do not think it is the proper course to send it to the Railway Committee, and I must ask the House to reject the motion of the Minister of Justice.

MCCARTHY (North Simcoe) moved second reading of Bill (No. 6) to amend the Steamboat Inspection Act of 1898. He said : The object of the Bill is to remedy a grievance which the marine engineers allege to have existed for some time past. They complain that the department, which now has power to issue permits, are thereby enabled to grant to men, who have not passed examination, certificates for the season to act as marine engineers. I have introduced this same Bill for two consecutive sessions. Last session it did not reach its second reading and the session before I agreed, owing to some objections, to allow it to stand. The Bill has since been pretty well circulated throughout the districts interested; and from what I have heard from the marine engineers themselves, the lumbermen who own tugs, and the fishermen who require tugs in their business, they desire to be Mr. LANCASTER.
given a hearing before a committee of the House. Since introducing the Bill I have found that there is a good deal of difference of opinion among the interests concerned, and after consultation with my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I came to the conclusion that the wisest course would be to have a small special committee which would hear the parties interested and report to the House. Were we to discuss the matter here, I am afraid there would be much difficulty in arriving at a satisfactory conclusion. From what I have heard from the different interests in my own constituency, it may be somewhat difficult to deal with the matter, and in justice to all parties interested, unless we hear from each class of persons what they have to say, the conclusion I have come to therefore is that the only satisfactory way to dispose of it would be to have the various parties interested brought before a special committee.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
